Imagine a village of 512 people. Fields, bakeries, theatres, two banks. Everyone needs two loaves a month; three months without bread, and you die. Now imagine I build it twice, identical, and change one thing: where the money comes from. Then I run each village for ten years, ten times over, and count who still has bread.

In the first village money is what it is for us: it is born when a bank makes a loan, and every coin in your pocket is a coin someone else owes. In the second, everyone receives a fixed income every month — five units — and money that sits idle above a small cushion pays a parking fee: two percent a month simply disappears. Nobody owes anyone for it. That's the whole difference.

I don't switch everything on at once. Bare fields first. Then a government. A theatre. A stock market. Cooperatives. Taxes. One rung at a time, both villages, same rung, and at every rung: who is alive, what does bread cost, what does the government owe.

Bare fields, no government. In the debt village, a hundred and fifty people are left after ten years. There is no work for most of them, without work no money, without money no bread. In the SuMSy village four hundred and fifty-eight live — and about twenty are hungry in any month: five units is half a meal, and half a meal keeps you alive only while someone hires you. Same fields, same bakers. Only the money, and who gets the work.

Add a government: public jobs and a bread allowance for the unemployed. Now almost everyone lives — and the government borrows half of what it spends, every month, for ten years, and never repays. Balance the books by taxing, and two hundred of five hundred and twelve are left. The debt village lives *because* its government goes into debt. And it can never get out: in that village, every coin in circulation is someone's debt.

It does — once. While the new money is still filling up the village, the parking tax brings in little, and the SuMSy government borrows its citizens' savings: about a month of guaranteed income per villager, at its worst in month six. Then it pays every unit back, by month thirty-three, in every run. A startup cost. One village repays; the other cannot. And from that step on, nobody in the SuMSy village is out of work — not one person, in ten years, in any run.

Now firms get owners, and shares that trade. In the debt village the gap between the richest tenth and the poorest is five hundred and seventy meals. In the SuMSy village, without a fee on land, it is ten thousand — and it is all land, hoarded because money melts and land doesn't. With the land fee paid out to everyone, two hundred and forty. With cooperatives, a hundred and sixty-six. The money system is not the whole story. Ownership is the other half, and land is a third.

Land. In the debt village a plot sells for thirty years of rent. In the SuMSy village, nobody sells — because money melts and land doesn't, so land becomes the thing to hold, and the rare sale goes for a fortune: seven hundred years of rent. Silvio Gesell saw this a century ago. The fix is a fee on land, paid out to everyone as a dividend: then land trades again, at four years of rent, the dividend is larger than the income itself, and the poorest tenth of the village hold sixteen meals instead of one.

Then I did something unkind: I made everyone greedy. Spend every surplus, forever. The SuMSy village dies — fifty-seven left on average, nobody in the worst run. Not through land this time: through bread. Everyone has money to spare, so the bread sells out; the bakeries bid for more grain than the land can grow; grain doubles, then doubles again; the bakeries' prices chase it at forty percent a year and never catch it; their bills go unpaid, and they are wound up one by one until the last one's closing starves the village. No rule saves it: let prices rise faster and it dies faster. The debt village under the same greed keeps five hundred and ten — its greedy have no spare money, and its prices stop where their money does. That is what a stress test is for: a village where everyone can always pay has nothing to ration bread with but hunger.

Ten years, ten runs, twelve rungs. What it takes to survive: in the debt village, a government willing to be permanently in debt, and a third of the village without work at every step. In the SuMSy village, an income everyone gets, a fee on idle money that pays for the state, a fee on land paid out as a dividend — and a labour market that shares the work, or the income alone leaves people behind. In both: taxes that stay off bread — the one tax that killed the village was the tax on bread. And the open question I can't answer yet: what happens in the ten years when you switch from one money to the other. That's the next simulation.

Everything here is a rule I chose, and every number comes from a run you can repeat: the code, the village and the report are public. I built one village and broke it a hundred ways. The question I'd leave you with isn't which money is better. It's this: every rule of money is a choice someone made. Which of them would you change?
